title: Token-length profiling and aligned-packer scheduling prototype
body:
Purpose
-------
This doc proposes a practical prototype called 'aligned-packer' that uses lightweight token-length profiling and input alignment heuristics to reduce wasted compute from padding and to improve kernel selection decisions. The idea is to bias scheduling toward groups of requests that share effective sequence-length buckets and prefix similarity, while incorporating KV-cache hit expectations to avoid rewarm costs.

Motivation / Background
-----------------------
Current problems we observe in production:
- High variance in input lengths across user requests causes poor packing efficiency and large padding overhead.
- Kernel choice (FP16 vs Q4_0 vs int8) is typically made at a coarse model-level; we could pick fastpaths that are length-aware.
- KV cache warm costs when routing requests to different workers reduce throughput for chat-style workloads.
- Existing bucketing systems either create too many strict bins (fragmentation) or too coarse bins (padding waste).

Design goals
------------
- Reduce per-token compute wasted on padding by 20–40% for mixed-length workloads.
- Make kernel selection sensitive to sequence-length distribution and expected prefix reuse.
- Keep runtime scheduling code simple: no global reordering that breaks fairness SLAs.
- Provide measurable signals to Optimize and Console for cost/latency tradeoffs.

Principles
----------
- Profile cheaply at admission: sample token length distribution per source (route/API key) using exponential decay counters.
- Compute an "aligned-length" target per short window (e.g., 1000 requests or 1 minute) that represents the 75th percentile length for that source.
- Assign an "alignment class" which is a small set of canonical lengths (e.g., 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024).
- Pack requests by alignment class first, then by prefix-similarity bucket (hash of last N tokens) with affinity scoring that considers KV cache hit probability.

Admission path heuristic (pseudo)
--------------------------------
1) Request arrives with seq_len L and route R.
2) Update per-route length sketch: counts[R].add(L).
3) Determine class C = nearest_canonical(L) (tie -> round up).
4) Compute prefix_hash = hash(top-k tokens).
5) Compute affinity = w1 * cache_hit_prob(R, prefix_hash) + w2 * (1 - fractional_padding(L, C)).
6) Place request in queue bucket (C, prefix_hash_modN) with score affinity.

Notes on canonical lengths and fractional_padding
- canonical lengths chosen to align with common attention/kernel tiling sizes and small-power-of-two-friendly memory layouts (e.g., 32/64/128/256).
- fractional_padding(L, C) = (C - L) / C, clipped to [0,1]. Lower is better.

Kernel selection policy
-----------------------
- Use a short-window profile to decide kernel fastpath per worker for each canonical class.
- If typical sequences in class C are < 128 tokens and cache_hit_prob > 0.6 -> prefer quantized kernels that have better throughput for short sequences.
- If class C contains many long-tail requests or large KV reuse costs -> prefer FP16 kernels to avoid rewarm overhead because slower per-token may be cheaper overall when avoiding cache miss penalties.
- Expose a per-worker "preferred_kernel(C)" that the dispatcher uses when assigning packed batches.

KV cache integration
--------------------
- Maintain a light-weight LRU estimate at dispatcher (not full KV contents): for (worker, prefix_hash_modN) keep a small counter of hits.
- cache_hit_prob approximated by exponential moving average of observed hits for same (route, prefix_modN).
- When affinity suggests high cache reuse, prefer keeping requests on the same worker even if it increases short-term padding by one canonical level.

Packing semantics and fairness
------------------------------
- Batching loop picks top-K affinity queues under each class where sum tokens in batch <= batch_token_limit.
- To preserve fairness across routes, implement weighted round-robin across routes within the same class with max-shot bias so a hot route can’t starve others.

Observability / Metrics
-----------------------
Add the following dashboards and derived metrics:
- per-route alignment distribution (hist of L vs canonical).
- padding_waste = sum(C - L) / sum(C) at 1m/5m windows per route.
- kernel_fastpath_hit_rate per class and per worker.
- cache_affinity_gain = latency/cost improvement measured when affinity chosen vs baseline routing.
- rewarm_penalty_estimate: count of requests that lost KV cache and incurred >X ms tail.

Experimental plan
-----------------
Phase 0: offline replay
- Run offline replay of historical traces with the allocation heuristic to estimate padding_waste reduction and KV cache dynamics.
- Compare against existing bucketing (current implementation) and aggressive tiny-bins approach.

Phase 1: Canary (internal only)
- Enable aligned-packer in canary region on a subset of workers and for a small set of routes (low-risk customers).
- Run A/B: 10% traffic gets aligned-packer vs 90% baseline. Measure p50/p95 latency, cost per 1M tokens, and cache miss counts.

Phase 2: Gradual rollout
- Open to more routes after 2 weeks of stable gains. Provide opt-out flag per-customer.

Implementation notes / Effort estimate
------------------------------------
- Admission path changes + per-route sketch: 1.5 engineer-weeks.
- Dispatcher queue changes (affinity bucket): 2 engineer-weeks.
- Kernel preference plumbing + metrics: 1 engineer-week.
- Canary infra + dashboards: 1 engineer-week.
Total: ~6 engineer-weeks to produce a working canary.

Open questions / Risks
---------------------
- Canonical lengths: how many classes before fragmentation? Start with 6, tune via replay.
- Cache estimate correctness: approximating cache probability may mislead affinity selection for highly bursty prefixes.
- Model-specific kernel characteristics: need to ensure we have per-model perf curves by length to automate kernel picks.

Next steps
----------
- Run replay job on traces from last 30 days (ticket JIRA-RT-8421).
- Prototype admission sketch and queueing in local dev environment; prepare benchmark harness.
- Sync with Kernel team about perf curves for quantized paths (action: @Ethan Zhao).

Appendix: simple pseudo-code for batch builder
--------------------------------------------
function build_batch(class C):
  candidates = top_queues_for_class(C, limit=16)
  sorted = sort_by_affinity_desc(candidates)
  batch = []
  tok_sum = 0
  for q in sorted:
    r = q.peek()
    if tok_sum + r.seq_len <= batch_token_limit:
      batch.append(q.pop())
      tok_sum += r.seq_len
    if tok_sum >= batch_token_limit: break
  return batch

Contributors: Priya Singh (author), Ethan Zhao (KV-cache sketch), Marta López (metrics), Noah Patel (kernel perf)
